Phonograph records and mechanical devices like tweezers and string could be used
Police relied on fingerprinting, witness testimony, and psychological deduction

surface_summary: Margaret Odell, a famous Broadway beauty known as the Canary, was strangled in her locked apartment which appeared ransacked as if by a professional burglar. The side door was bolted from the inside, and no one was seen entering or leaving, creating a baffling locked-room mystery. Several suspects with motives and alibis were investigated, including a burglar who was later found strangled himself.
accepted_facts: Margaret Odell was strangled in her apartment late at night
The side door to the building was bolted from the inside all night
Tony Skeel’s fingerprints were found in the apartment and he had a key
A phonograph record was used to fake screams heard by the telephone operator
inferred_conclusions: Tony Skeel was the murderer because of his fingerprints and criminal record
William Elmer Jessup (Benton) was guilty due to his access and nervousness
The crime was a simple burglary gone wrong
mechanism_description: Kenneth Spotswoode murdered Margaret Odell to prevent her from ruining his life through blackmail. He staged the crime to appear as a professional burglary, using a phonograph record to fake screams heard by the telephone operator. He manipulated the locked side door with a string and tweezers device to create an alibi, hiding his presence and movements, but was ultimately exposed by Philo Vance’s psychological deductions and demonstration.
delivery_path: Spotswoode unbolted the side door from outside using tweezers and string
He entered the apartment quietly before Odell and her escort returned
Hid in the clothes-press while Odell and Spotswoode’s escort were present
Strangled Odell after the escort left and staged the burglary scene
Set the phonograph record with screams to play after leaving
Rebolted the side door from inside using the tweezers and string
Left the apartment and established an alibi by going to the club
outcome_result: Kenneth Spotswoode was arrested for the murder of Margaret Odell and subsequently committed suicide.

false_assumption.statement: The side door was bolted all night and could not have been unbolted and rebolted without detection.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The janitor and witnesses testified the door was bolted early and remained so, and no one was seen entering or leaving through it. The telephone operators also confirmed no unauthorized passage.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It hides the possibility that the murderer used a mechanical device to unbolt and rebolt the door silently and remotely, allowing secret entry and exit.

supporting_points: His fingerprints were found on the closet door and table
He had a key to the side door
He suddenly quit his job and planned to flee
He had a criminal record and motive due to infatuation
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He could not have unbolted and rebolted the side door without detection, and the physical and psychological evidence did not fit him as the murderer.

red_herrings.description: Charles Cleaver was blackmailed by Odell and had a suspicious alibi involving a speeding summons from another town.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Cleaver fabricated the alibi and was not present at the time of the murder; his involvement was limited to blackmail and personal grievances.

red_herrings.description: Doctor Lindquist was infatuated and jealous of Odell, threatened her, and had a weak alibi.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Lindquist was hospitalized during the second murder and his alibi was confirmed; his threats were emotional outbursts without murderous intent.

closed_circle.rationale: These four men were the only intimate acquaintances of Margaret Odell with potential motives and opportunity, forming the complete set of plausible suspects.

time_anchors: Monday night between 10 p.m. and midnight
Half past eleven when Odell was last seen alive
Five minutes to twelve when Cleaver was seen leaving
Ten minutes to twelve when the phone call was made
time_windows: Odell and Spotswoode returned at about 11 p.m.
Skeel hid in closet during Odell’s return and murder
Spotswoode left apartment at about 11:35 p.m.

access_objects: Side door with bolt and tweezers-string device
authority_sources: Captain Dubois and Detective Bellamy (fingerprint experts)

inference_path.observation: Side door was bolted from inside all night according to janitor and police
inference_path.correction: Vance demonstrated that the door could be unbolted and rebolted from outside using tweezers and string
inference_path.effect: Allowed secret entry and exit, disproving the locked-door alibi
required_evidence: Tweezers with purple twine found in Skeel’s waistcoat pocket
Demonstration of door bolt manipulation at Odell apartment

inference_path.observation: Screams heard by telephone operator Jessup at about 11:35 p.m.
inference_path.correction: Screams were phonograph recordings played by Spotswoode to fake a live disturbance
inference_path.effect: Phonograph record created false alibi and misled investigators
required_evidence: Phonograph record of screams found in Odell apartment
Jessup’s testimony about timing of screams and calls

inference_path.observation: Tony Skeel’s fingerprints found in apartment and he had a key
inference_path.correction: Skeel was hiding in the clothes-press closet during the murder and was a terrified witness, not the murderer
inference_path.effect: Skeel’s presence explained fingerprints but exonerated him from murder
required_evidence: Fingerprints on closet door knob matching Skeel
Skeel’s alibi and behavior during interrogation

inference_path.observation: Cleaver had a speeding summons from Boonton as alibi
inference_path.correction: Traffic officer who issued summons identified a different man, indicating Cleaver’s alibi was fabricated
inference_path.effect: Cleaver’s alibi was false, increasing suspicion but not proving guilt
required_evidence: Traffic officer Phipps’s testimony and description

inference_path.observation: Spotswoode had an alibi playing poker until 3 a.m.
inference_path.correction: Vance’s psychological poker test showed Spotswoode’s high self-confidence and risk-taking matched the murderer’s profile
inference_path.effect: Psychological evidence implicated Spotswoode despite physical alibi
required_evidence: Poker game with Spotswoode, Vance, Cleaver, Allen, and Markham
Vance’s analysis of betting behavior and bluff

inference_path.observation: Phonograph record played screams after murder
inference_path.correction: Spotswoode prepared the record to create an alibi and mislead witnesses
inference_path.effect: Demonstrated premeditation and deception by Spotswoode
required_evidence: Phonograph and record found in Odell apartment

inference_path.observation: Jewelry found in trash can across town
inference_path.correction: Spotswoode discarded the jewelry to fake burglary and mislead police
inference_path.effect: Further evidence of Spotswoode’s attempt to stage the crime
required_evidence: Mannix’s knowledge of jewelry and Furriers’ Club newspapers

discriminating_test.design: Vance invited the main suspects to a poker game to observe their psychological traits and risk-taking behavior. Spotswoode’s daring bluff and high-stakes betting revealed a personality consistent with the murderer’s profile, while others were eliminated by their more cautious or inconsistent play.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The test revealed Spotswoode’s supreme self-confidence and willingness to risk everything, matching the psychological profile of the killer.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The suspect’s betting behavior must demonstrate calculated risk-taking and bluffing consistent with the murderer's psychological profile, distinguishing him from more cautious suspects.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given detailed descriptions of the apartment layout, the locked side door, the phonograph record, the suspects’ alibis and motives, and the psychological profiles. Clues such as the tweezers and string device, the phonograph record, and the poker game are all presented before the solution. The reader could deduce the mechanism of the door bolt trick and suspect Spotswoode’s psychological profile as the key to the crime.
